transcript.text: Our client is LedgerLoop, which sells accounting software to small businesses. It has built an AI assistant that categorizes expenses automatically. How should LedgerLoop price the new feature?
I think they should just charge 10 dollars because that sounds reasonable.
What would you want to learn before settling on a price? Please lay out how you’d evaluate the options, then we can dig into the data.
Okay, I guess I'd look at costs and competitors. What does the feature cost to run?
It costs LedgerLoop about $2 per customer per month to run the feature. What would you like to investigate next?
QuickBooks includes a similar feature in its $90-a-month plan, while Xero charges $15 a month for an add-on. How would you use that information to assess LedgerLoop’s pricing options?
So Xero is 15, so maybe 15 is fine.

That’s a useful reference point, but competitors’ prices don’t tell us what LedgerLoop’s customers will pay or what the feature is worth to them. What would you want to learn next to test whether $15 is the right price?
How many customers would buy it?
In a survey, 40% of customers said they’d add it at $10 a month, compared with 20% at $20. I’m putting an exhibit on your screen. How would you compare the revenue at those two prices?
At 10 dollars maybe 40 percent buy, at 20 dollars 20 percent buy. I would pick 10 dollars because more people buy it.
More customers would buy at $10, but that alone doesn’t tell us which price earns more. Compare monthly revenue per 100 customers at each price, then account for the $2 monthly cost per buyer.
The CEO just walked in. Please give your final recommendation, including why you’d choose that price and how you’d protect retention.

math_results.question: How much is the feature worth to a typical customer each month?
What monthly profit does the feature make at $10?
What monthly profit does the feature make at $20?

scorecard.top_strength: You recognized competitor pricing as a useful reference point and asked what competitors charge.
scorecard.biggest_gap: You did not compare contribution profit at $10 and $20, so your choice relied on adoption volume alone rather than the case’s core economics.
scorecard.summary: You identified costs, competitor pricing, and adoption as relevant inputs, but you did not calculate customer value or compare the profits at the two tested prices. You should structure the analysis around cost, competitive anchors, customer value, and adoption economics, then recommend a price with a retention safeguard and a clear test plan.
